cim: Ethnoeducation, Afro-descendant youth leadership, and artificial intelligence literacy: an exploratory study with educational actors from Esmeraldas, Ecuador
cim_eredeti: Ethnoeducation, Afro-descendant youth leadership, and artificial intelligence literacy: an exploratory study with educational actors from Esmeraldas, Ecuador
szoveg_eredeti:
Volume 11 - 2026 | https://doi.org/10.3389/feduc.2026.1910214

Universidad Politécnica Salesiana, Quito, Ecuador

This study examines artificial intelligence (AI) literacy and educommunication as central dimensions in educational processes related to Afro-descendant youth leadership in Ecuador.

An exploratory study with an explanatory-sequential mixed-methods design was conducted. In the quantitative phase, an online survey was administered to 90 participants involved in educational, youth, and community processes, predominantly in the province of Esmeraldas (94.4% of the sample), with a small number of participants from Santo Domingo de los Tsáchilas. Descriptive statistics, internal-consistency estimates, and exploratory Spearman rank-order correlations between dimension scores were calculated. The qualitative phase consisted of a virtual focus group with three young Afro-Ecuadorian participants selected to deepen specific survey findings.

The survey showed high agreement across six dimensions, with Afro-descendant identity receiving the highest mean and critical AI literacy the lowest relative mean. Reliability varied substantially across dimensions. Exploratory bivariate results showed positive moderate-to-strong associations among the six dimension scores, interpreted as associations rather than causal effects. Qualitative findings showed selective and cautious AI use and documented experiences of racialized digital representation, identity reaffirmation, and demand for ethical, community-based AI training. The qualitative phase elaborated and qualified the quantitative patterns rather than merely reproducing them.

The findings support a culturally situated approach to AI literacy that combines technical understanding, ethical judgment, cultural recognition, and educommunicative production. The findings are exploratory and non-generalizable but provide an empirically grounded framework for future educational interventions and measurement research in Afro-descendant and intercultural contexts.

Educational, communicative, and cultural practices are being reshaped by the expansion of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI). In educational settings, its use has extended to writing support, information retrieval, content production, feedback, assessment, and personalized learning. However, these dynamics cannot be interpreted solely as technological changes, since they directly affect how knowledge is produced, validated, communicated, and socially recognized.

UNESCO (2023) argues that the integration of GenAI into education should be guided by human-centered approaches to ensure ethical, inclusive, and privacy-respecting practices that strengthen the agency of teachers and students, thereby avoiding the uncritical adoption of automated systems. Along these lines, international AI competency frameworks emphasize the simultaneous development of technical, ethical, and pedagogical competencies for the responsible integration of AI into teaching and learning processes (UNESCO, 2024).

In Latin America, this phenomenon is particularly significant, as digital transformations are unfolding in contexts marked by social inequalities, educational gaps, and uneven access to technology. Accordingly, the regional digital divide is not limited to connectivity or equipment; it also encompasses digital competencies, critical capacities, and forms of participation in digital educational environments (Herrera et al., 2025; Vuorikari et al., 2022).

For Afro-descendant peoples and communities, this scenario becomes more complex because of historical exclusion, structural racism, statistical invisibility, stereotyped representation, and limited access to public decision-making spaces. For this reason, digital literacy and AI literacy must be framed through an intercultural and situated perspective that responds to the specific realities of these communities. In this regard, the Economic Commission for Latin America and the Caribbean (ECLAC, 2020) argues that recognizing the rights of Afro-descendant populations is essential to building more just, equal, and democratic societies.

In Ecuador, the provinces of Esmeraldas, Imbabura, Guayas, Pichincha, Carchi, and El Oro have the largest Afro-descendant populations in the country, reflecting a significant historical, cultural, and territorial presence. Nevertheless, their forms of leadership, memory, spirituality, community organization, and cultural production are often subordinated to dominant, folklorizing, or oversimplified narratives. In this context, AI may open opportunities by expanding the production of self-defined narratives, while also posing risks through the reproduction of biases, stereotypes, and forms of algorithmic exclusion, as critical studies on algorithms, race, and power have warned (Noble, 2018).

This study examines the intersection of AI literacy, educommunication, and Afro-descendant youth leadership in Ecuador by addressing the following research question:

How can educommunicative practices supported by artificial intelligence strengthen Afro-descendant youth leadership in intercultural educational contexts in Ecuador?

In this study, AI literacy is understood not merely as the ability to use AI-based tools, but as a situated communicative practice through which historically marginalized groups can critically interpret algorithmic environments, question biases, produce culturally meaningful narratives, and strengthen collective educational agency. This perspective aligns with approaches that conceptualize AI literacy as a set of critical, communicative, and practical competencies for engaging with intelligent systems in everyday life (Long and Magerko, 2020).

The contribution of this study lies at the intersection of communication, education, and applied technologies through the proposal of a culturally situated model of AI literacy aimed at strengthening Afro-descendant youth leadership.

Artificial intelligence literacy is a key concept for understanding how teachers and students can develop a critical relationship with intelligent systems. Long and Magerko (2020) define it as a set of competencies that enables individuals to evaluate AI technologies, communicate effectively about them, and use them as tools for technical, administrative, educational, and communicative support in everyday life.

This perspective suggests that AI literacy is not intended to turn everyone into programmers or computer specialists. Rather, it entails developing the capacity to recognize the possibilities and limitations of AI, assess its outputs, identify embedded biases, and make informed decisions about when and in which contexts its use is appropriate (Long and Magerko, 2020; UNESCO, 2024).

AI literacy should also be connected to broader digital competence frameworks, such as DigComp 2.2, which defines digital competence as a combination of knowledge, skills, and attitudes that enable safe and responsible participation in digital environments (Vuorikari et al., 2022). The use of AI, therefore, is not merely instrumental; it is also social, communicative, and ethical.

From this perspective, AI literacy involves at least four types of competencies: (i) critical competence, understood as the ability to evaluate AI-generated information, verify sources, and identify errors; (ii) ethical competence, associated with the recognition of biases, privacy risks, and forms of discrimination; (iii) narrative competence, related to the use of digital and intelligent tools to produce stories, content, and messages; and (iv) participatory competence, which refers to the use of digital and intelligent environments for leadership, community organization, and civic participation (ECLAC, 2020; Noble, 2018).
